The bottle arrived on the third tide of November, tumbling against the rocks below with a sound like knuckles on a door. Maren fished it from the surf with her hook, and inside, rolled tight as a secret, was a slip of paper.

She unrolled it. Read it. Read it again.

*Don't light the lamp on the 14th.*

Her own handwriting. She knew it the way she knew the creak of the spiral stairs, the taste of tin in the rainwater cistern. The same loops and slants she used to sign the logbook each morning.

But she hadn't written this. She hadn't.

Maren checked the date. November 13th.

She climbed the tower that night and sat beside the lens, watching the sea churn black beneath a moonless sky. Ships would come. Ships always came when the light failed. She knew this. She had seen the wrecks stacked like broken teeth along the shoals.

But the handwriting was hers. The warning was hers.

At midnight, she lifted the oil can.

Somewhere far out in the dark, something waited to see what she would choose—and Maren realized, with a cold and certain dread, that it had been waiting a long time.
